meta.title: Who really said "I never met a man I didn't like"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Will Rogers. He called it "my old saying" in his syndicated column of 20 February 1927 — and the famous form trims a longer tombstone line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I never met a man I didn't like'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Will Rogers. He called it "my old saying" in his column of 20 February 1927 — the famous form trims a longer tombstone line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1879–1935 · Cherokee cowboy humorist, syndicated columnist & film star
answer.sourceLine: Rogers put the exact words in print himself. In weekly article no. 219, “Rogers Gets Six Shiny Dimes From Oil King,” published in the Tulsa Daily World on 20 February 1927, he writes that John D. Rockefeller “sure carried out my old saying, ‘I never met a man I didn’t like.’” He was already calling it an old saying then — and he was still using it three years later when he offered it, in a longer form, as his own epitaph.

source.excerpt: He gave me my dimes all of them and I didn’t even ask him. Well, I might have hinted a little. He is a Baptist, but he certainly is not a narrow one. For there was Father Lennon, who he spoke so often of, what a “fine man Father was.” John D. sure carried out my old saying, “I never met a man I didn’t like.”
trail: 6 November 1926 — the earliest dated version yet found. Writing about having missed Leon Trotsky in Russia, Rogers says he would have found him “a very interesting and human fellow, for I never yet met a man that I dident like.” Wikiquote ↗ attributes it to the Saturday Evening Post and notes Rogers’ own spelling.

20 February 1927 — the exact modern wording, in Rogers’ own syndicated weekly article no. 219 on John D. Rockefeller: “John D. sure carried out my old saying, ‘I never met a man I didn’t like.’” Weekly Articles, Vol. 2 ↗

16 June 1930 — the epitaph version goes national. Under the headline “Will Rogers Likes Everyone,” page one of the New Britain Herald reports that Rogers told an audience at Tremont Temple Baptist Church in Boston the night before what he had prepared for his tombstone. Library of Congress ↗
29 June 1930 — Rogers explains the line, tying it to how he got away with kidding public men: “I have always said I never met a man I dident like.” Weekly Articles, Vol. 4 ↗
source.excerptNote: Rogers had played a show at Daytona Beach the night before, and the 87-year-old John D. Rockefeller was in the audience; he asked Rogers to breakfast at eight the next morning and handed out his famous dimes at the door — six of them, one for Rogers and one each for his wife, his three children and his sister. He did not play the golf that followed — “I told him I didn’t play but that I would go over with them” — and picked up one more dime for watching. Note that he introduces the line as “my old saying” — it was already stock by early 1927.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: The man who said it
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · Cherokee humorist, roper, syndicated columnist & film star
author.bio: Born in 1879 near Oologah in Indian Territory, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, Will Rogers went from trick roper in wild west shows to the Ziegfeld Follies, then to Hollywood and to the biggest newspaper readership in America. Between 1922 and his death he wrote thousands of syndicated weekly articles and daily telegrams, needling presidents, senators and oil barons in the voice of a man who had wandered in from the corral. He died on 15 August 1935 in a plane crash in Alaska Territory with the aviator Wiley Post.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: Nobody else has a serious claim on this sentence — the trouble is with its shape, its date, and with Rogers himself, who at some point tried to disown it.

items.who: “I joked about every prominent man of my time…”
items.why: The famous epitaph sentence circulates with “of my time.” The wire report of the Boston remark carried on page one of the New Britain Herald for 16 June 1930 prints “lifetime” instead — “I joked about every prominent man in my lifetime, but I never met a man I didn’t like” (Library of Congress ↗). Wikiquote lists both forms.

Rogers spelled it his own way. Wikiquote flags the 1926 version as deliberately “dident,” and his weekly article published 29 June 1930 reads “I never met a man I dident like” (Weekly Articles, Vol. 4 ↗). The 1927 column is printed with the standard spelling.

items.who: “He first said it in Boston in 1930”
items.why: That claim traces to Paula McSpadden Love’s The Will Rogers Book (1972), which says the remark was first printed in the Boston Globe of 16 June 1930. Wikiquote quotes her note and then records earlier uses — the 1926 Trotsky remark and the 1927 column (Wikiquote ↗).

items.who: Will Rogers, disowning his own line
items.why: In the London Review of Books, Michael Rogin wrote that “Will Rogers denied ever uttering his signature phrase” and that Rogers claimed his actual words were “I never kidded a man I didn’t like” (LRB ↗). His own columns undercut the denial — and show why the two versions blur together, since he used the “met” form precisely to explain his kidding.

misattribution.truthLine: The line really is Rogers’. He was calling it “my old saying” in a column published 20 February 1927 ↗; what travels is a trimmed, tidied fragment of the longer sentence he wanted on his tombstone.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Rogers made a living ridiculing the most powerful men in America — presidents, senators, Rockefeller — and somehow kept being invited back. The line was his own explanation of the trick. In a weekly article published in the Tulsa Daily World on 29 June 1930 he set it out plainly: he had “often said in answer to inquiries as to how I got away with kidding some of our public men, that it was because I liked all of them personally, and that if there was no malice in your heart there could be none in your ‘Gags,’ and I have always said I never met a man I dident like.” (Weekly Articles, Vol. 4 ↗)

Stripped of that setup, the sentence turns into a greeting-card sentiment about universal goodwill. In its native habitat it is a working humorist’s licence — the reason a cowboy from Indian Territory could call a sitting president a fool in 500 newspapers and be thanked for it.
detailsBody: Wikiquote records an earlier and slightly different form: writing about having missed Leon Trotsky on his 1926 trip to Russia, Rogers said he would have found him “a very interesting and human fellow, for I never yet met a man that I dident like.” Wikiquote dates that to the Saturday Evening Post of 6 November 1926 and calls it “the earliest dated citation of such a remark thus far found in research” (Wikiquote ↗).
By February 1927 the sentence had settled into the shape everyone knows, and Rogers was introducing it as something he had been saying for a while.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section lists "I never met a man I didn't like" citing nationally syndicated column no. 219, "Rogers Gets Six Shiny Dimes From Oil King" (1927); quotes Paula McSpadden Love's note that the epitaph remark was first printed in the Boston Globe, June 16, 1930, after Rogers spoke at Tremont Temple Baptist Church; records the variant "I joked about every prominent man in my lifetime, but I never met one I didn't like"; and states that the earliest dated citation of such a remark found in research is the 1926 Trotsky remark from the Saturday Evening Post (6 November 1926), "I never yet met a man that I dident like", noting Rogers specifically spelled the word "dident".

The Will Rogers Memorial Museums' online edition of Will Rogers' Weekly Articles, Volume 2: The Coolidge Years, 1925-1927 contains article no. 219, "Rogers Gets Six Shiny Dimes From Oil King", whose text reads "John D. sure carried out my old saying, 'I never met a man I didn't like.'", and whose editorial note dates it "TDW, February 20, 1927" (Tulsa Daily World).

Will Rogers' Weekly Articles, Volume 4: The Hoover Years, 1929-1931 contains article no. 392, "Will and Sharkey Talk It Over", reading "I have often said in answer to inquiries as to how I got away with kidding some of our public men, that it was because I liked all of them personally, and that if there was no malice in your heart there could be none in your 'Gags,' and I have always said I never met a man I dident like." The editorial note gives "published: TDW, June 29, 1930".

Page 1 of the New Britain Herald (New Britain, Conn.) for June 16, 1930 carries an item headed "Will Rogers Likes Everyone" reading (per the Library of Congress OCR) "...joked about every prominent man ... lifetime but ... never met ... man ... didn['t] like ... the epitaph which Will Rogers had prepared for his tombstone ... told [an] audience [at] Tremont Temple Bapti[s]t Church last night."

The Library of Congress word-coordinates (ALTO OCR) service for page segment /service/ndnp/ct/batch_ct_inxs_ver01/data/sn82014519/00414183542/1930061601/0919.xml returns the text of the New Britain Herald front page of 16 June 1930, including the "Will Rogers Likes Everyone" item with the epitaph wording and the Tremont Temple Baptist Church reference — this is the fetch that confirmed the newspaper page's content.

Michael Rogin's London Review of Books essay states: "Will Rogers denied ever uttering his signature phrase, 'I never met a man I didn't like.' 'I never kidded a man I didn't like' were his actual words, he claimed." It adds that the only time he is on record using the more familiar tag-line is on a 1926 visit to the Soviet Union, regretting having missed Leon Trotsky.

The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture entry for William Penn Adair Rogers gives his birth as November 4, 1879 in Indian Territory near Oologah and his death as August 15, 1935 in a plane crash near Barrow, Alaska, describes his career (vaudeville, Ziegfeld Follies, seventy-one motion pictures, columns syndicated to over 500 papers), and states he ordered his own epitaph: "I joked about every prominent man of my time, but I never met a man I didn't like."

Wikipedia's Will Rogers article gives his birth (November 4, 1879, near Oologah, Indian Territory), death (August 15, 1935, Alaska Territory plane crash), Cherokee Nation citizenship, career (trick roper, Ziegfeld Follies 1915-1925, 71 films, more than 4,000 syndicated columns from 1922), and states "One of Rogers's most famous sayings was 'I never met a man I didn't like'", quoting his epitaph remark with his own spelling "dident".

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum WRITINGS page describes and links free PDF editions of Rogers' Daily Telegrams and six volumes of Weekly Articles, and notes he published six books and over 3,600 newspaper columns.
